V0001.line: GS2 | Polity | Salient features of the Representation of People's Act
V0001.title: Representation of the People Act 1950, UPSC Notes
facts: RPA 1950 covers seat allocation for Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Councils, delimitation, voter qualifications, electoral rolls and the manner of filling seats.
Its four Schedules: First, Lok Sabha seats and SC/ST reservation; Second, Assembly strength per State; Third, Council seats; Fourth, local authorities electing to Councils.
Articles 82 and 170 require Lok Sabha and Assembly seats to be readjusted after each census.
A voter must be 18 on the qualifying date and ordinarily resident in the constituency; nobody may be enrolled in two constituencies or twice in one.
Barred from registration: non-citizens, persons declared of unsound mind by a competent court, and persons disqualified under corrupt-practice or election-offence laws.
Each State's Chief Electoral Officer, designated by the ECI in consultation with the State, supervises preparation, revision and correction of all rolls.
The District Election Officer coordinates roll work in a district; the Electoral Registration Officer prepares and revises each constituency's roll.
A Parliamentary constituency's roll is made up of the rolls of all its Assembly constituencies, prepared under ECI superintendence.
Election Laws (Amendment) Act 2021: Aadhaar may be sought to establish identity, four qualifying dates a year (1 Jan, 1 Apr, 1 Jul, 1 Oct), 'spouse' replaces 'wife'.
Civil courts cannot decide a person's entitlement to be enrolled or question an ERO's action; roll offences by officers need an ECI or CEO complaint.
The Law Commission supports the ECI proposal of a common electoral roll for Parliament, Assembly and local body elections.

V0005.line: GS2 | Polity | Salient features of the Representation of People's Act
V0005.title: Ordinarily Resident, Meaning, Rules, Definition
facts: Section 19 of RPA 1950 allows enrolment only of a person ordinarily resident in the constituency.
Section 20 defines ordinarily resident: merely owning or possessing a house in a constituency does not make a person ordinarily resident there.
Spouses of persons with a service qualification are also treated as ordinarily resident in the original constituency.
Section 20A, added in 2010, lets Non-Resident Indians register at the address in their passport while living abroad.

V0006.line: GS2 | Polity | Constitutional posts and bodies: appointment, powers, functions, responsibilities
V0006.title: Article 324 of the Constitution, Key Provisions, Powers & Functions
facts: Article 324(1) vests superintendence, direction and control of electoral rolls and of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President in the ECI.
Article 324(2): the ECI is the CEC plus such number of Election Commissioners as the President fixes; appointments are subject to any law made by Parliament.
Article 324(3): the CEC acts as Chairman of the Commission when other Election Commissioners are appointed.
Article 324(5): the CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge, and his service conditions cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment.
Other Election Commissioners and Regional Commissioners can be removed only on the recommendation of the CEC.
Article 324(6): the President or a Governor must provide the ECI or Regional Commissioners the staff they request.
CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023: President appoints on a committee of PM, Lok Sabha LoP and a PM-nominated Cabinet Minister.
Under the 2023 Act, appointees must hold or have held a post equal to Secretary to the Government of India and have election-management experience.
Tenure of the CEC and ECs: six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier; they are not eligible for reappointment.
The 2023 Act followed Anoop Baranwal v Union of India (2023), where the SC had set an interim panel of PM, LoP and CJI, and repealed the 1991 Act.

V0007.line: GS2 | Polity | Constitutional posts and bodies: appointment, powers, functions, responsibilities
V0007.title: Election Commission of India (ECI), Structure, Framework, Composition
facts: The ECI is a permanent constitutional body under Article 324 supervising elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.
It was a single-member body until 1989 and has been a three-member body (CEC and two Election Commissioners) since October 1993.
All three members have equal powers, salary and status; decisions are taken by majority, with the CEC as head.
CEC removal needs a motion passed by a special majority in both Houses on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, as for a Supreme Court judge.
Delimitation is carried out by a separate Delimitation Commission set up by the Centre, not by the ECI.
The ECI prepares and revises electoral rolls, schedules polls, deploys polling staff and enforces the Model Code of Conduct.
S. Subramaniam Balaji v State of Tamil Nadu (2013): the SC asked the ECI to frame guidelines on election manifestos, later made part of the Model Code.
The Commission's staff is drawn from central and state government services.

V0008.line: GS3 | Environment | Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment
V0008.title: Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), Mechanism, Stages, Challenges
facts: GRAP was framed after Supreme Court directions in M.C. Mehta vs Union of India (2016) to tackle air pollution in Delhi-NCR.
The CPCB prepared GRAP in 2016 and the MoEFCC notified it in 2017.
EPCA, set up under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, first implemented GRAP; the Commission for Air Quality Management has implemented it since 2021.
A CAQM sub-committee of pollution-board officials, IMD and IITM scientists and health experts decides GRAP stages.
GRAP has four stages tied to AQI bands; measures of earlier stages continue when a higher stage is invoked.
Stage I (AQI 201-300, poor): dust control, mechanised sweeping, water sprinkling and a ban on open burning.
Stage II (AQI 301-400, very poor): ban on diesel generators except emergencies, higher parking fees, intensified enforcement.
Stage III (AQI 401-450, severe; can be invoked earlier on a rising trend): ban on non-essential construction, hot-mix plants, stone crushers and brick kilns.
Stage IV (AQI above 450, severe plus): entry of most diesel trucks barred, schools may shut, 50% staff work from home.
GRAP is preventive: IMD and IITM/SAFAR forecasts trigger stages before pollution peaks.

V0009.line: GS2 | Polity | Parliament and State legislatures: structure, functioning, conduct of business, powers and privileges
V0009.title: Public Accounts Committee, History, Members, Purpose
facts: The PAC, set up in 1921, is the oldest parliamentary committee in India and is constituted every year.
It has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha; the term is one year and Ministers cannot be members.
The Speaker appoints the Chairperson from its Lok Sabha members; by convention since 1967-68 the Chair is from the Opposition.
It examines CAG audit reports on appropriation accounts, finance accounts and public undertakings, and reports to Parliament.
It checks that money granted by Parliament was spent within the authorised limits and for the intended purpose, and probes losses and irregularities.
The PAC, Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings are Parliament's three financial standing committees.

V0010.line: GS2 | Polity | Parliament and State legislatures: structure, functioning, conduct of business, powers and privileges
V0010.title: Parliamentary Committees, Significance, UPSC Notes
facts: Parliamentary committees are appointed or elected by a House or nominated by the Speaker, work under the Speaker's direction and report to the House.
Estimates Committee: 30 members, all from Lok Sabha, one-year term; it suggests economies in public expenditure.
Committee on Public Undertakings: 22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha), one-year term; it examines reports and accounts of public sector undertakings.
Financial committee members are elected by proportional representation by single transferable vote.
Committees give specialised, less partisan scrutiny and can call officials to give evidence, strengthening executive accountability.

V0011.line: GS2 | Polity | Constitutional posts and bodies: appointment, powers, functions, responsibilities
V0011.title: Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), Article, Reports
facts: The CAG submits Union audit reports to the President, who has them laid before both Houses (Article 151); State reports go to the Governor.
The PAC examines CAG reports and reports its findings to Parliament; the CAG assists the PAC in this examination.
The CAG lists the most urgent audit matters for the PAC and explains officials' views to legislators and vice versa.
The CAG's service conditions cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment.
The administrative expenses of the CAG's office are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so they are not voted by Parliament.
Article 149 lets Parliament prescribe the CAG's duties and powers relating to the accounts of the Union and the States.

V0012.line: GS1 | Geography | Geophysical phenomena (earthquakes, tsunami, volcanoes, cyclones), geographical features and changes in critical features, flora and fauna
V0012.title: Cyclone
facts: Tropical cyclones form between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, usually near the ITCZ over warm oceans, and move heat from the equator towards the poles.
A tropical cyclone is a heat engine powered by the latent heat of condensation released as moist air rises.
Favourable conditions: sea surface above about 27°C, Coriolis force, small vertical wind shear and a pre-existing low-pressure area or circulation.
They are called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoons in the western North Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.
Temperate cyclones form in middle and high latitudes and do not occur over India.

V0013.line: GS1 | Geography | Geophysical phenomena (earthquakes, tsunami, volcanoes, cyclones), geographical features and changes in critical features, flora and fauna
V0013.title: Cyclone Nivar, Naming, Impact, Tropical Cyclones in India
facts: Tropical cyclones do not form between 5°N and 5°S because the Coriolis force there is too weak.
Upper-air divergence (high pressure aloft) keeps air rising and deepens the surface low; without it the system collapses.
Cold ocean currents prevent cyclones, so they are rare off the west coasts of South America, Africa and Australia.
North Indian Ocean cyclones are named by the WMO/ESCAP Panel of 13 countries: Bangladesh, India, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, UAE, Yemen.
The Bay of Bengal gets more cyclones than the Arabian Sea: warmer waters, and remnants of Pacific typhoons can re-intensify over it.
India's coastline of over 7,500 km makes it highly exposed to tropical cyclones.

V0014.line: GS1 | Geography | Geophysical phenomena (earthquakes, tsunami, volcanoes, cyclones), geographical features and changes in critical features, flora and fauna
V0014.title: Cyclone Shakti, Naming, Formation, Location, Classification
facts: IMD classes systems by sustained wind: cyclonic storm 62-88 km/h, severe cyclonic storm 89-117 km/h, very severe cyclonic storm 118-165 km/h.
Names come from lists contributed by the 13 member countries and are used in sequence under WMO and ESCAP Panel guidelines.
IMD's Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre in New Delhi tracks North Indian Ocean cyclones and issues forecasts.
The Indian scale corresponds to the international Saffir-Simpson scale but uses North Indian Ocean terminology.

V0015.line: GS2 | Polity | Executive and Judiciary: structure, organisation, functioning; Ministries and Departments; pressure groups
V0015.title: Capital Punishment in India, Background, Legal Provisions
facts: India retained the death penalty after 1950, subject to the safeguards of Article 21.
Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980) upheld the death penalty but confined it to the 'rarest of rare' cases.
Life imprisonment is the rule and death the exception; courts must weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
After appeals, review and curative petitions, a convict may seek mercy from the President (Article 72) or the Governor (Article 161).
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita provides death for offences such as murder, terrorism and rape resulting in death; execution is by hanging.

V0016.line: GS2 | Polity | Executive and Judiciary: structure, organisation, functioning; Ministries and Departments; pressure groups
V0016.title: Death Penalty in India - Appellate Courts Correcting Trial Court Errors
facts: A death sentence passed by a Sessions Court must be confirmed by the High Court; the convict can appeal to the Supreme Court.
No death sentence can be imposed on a person who was under 18 when the offence was committed.
Jagmohan Singh v State of UP (1973) upheld the constitutionality of the death penalty against challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 21.
Machhi Singh v State of Punjab (1983) laid down categories for applying the rarest of rare test, focusing on the crime.
The death penalty is valid under Article 21 only if the procedure is fair, just and reasonable.
